title: The 3 Requirements Of Real, Effective Time-Out
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin contends that most teachers don't keep students in time-out nearly long enough to produce real behavior change, arguing that fewer than fifteen minutes rarely gives a student time to calm down, reflect, feel remorse, and accept responsibility. He proposes three requirements a student must fulfill before returning to class: complete assigned work quietly during the initial period, take the initiative to raise a hand when ready, and verbally take responsibility for the misbehavior in a way that convinces the teacher it's sincere. The burden of proof, he stresses, rests on the student rather than the teacher. He ties the strategy back to a recurring theme on the site—that firm, non-negotiable boundaries combined with a classroom students genuinely enjoy being part of is what gives consequences like time-out real meaning and effect.
points: Fifteen minutes is a bare minimum for time-out to actually change behavior—five or ten rarely works.
Students must actively initiate their return (raising a hand) rather than the teacher deciding when they're done.
Require a sincere, self-articulated acknowledgment of responsibility before allowing a student back to their seat.
The burden of proof for readiness rests on the student, not the teacher—if unconvinced, leave them in time-out longer.
Time-out only works within a classroom students genuinely like being part of; otherwise the consequence has no weight.
quotes: If you’re like most teachers, you don’t keep your students in time-out long enough. For a majority of students, regardless of grade level, five or ten minutes won’t cut it.
Teachers often forget that time-out is meant to discourage future misbehavior. It’s not a formality. It’s not a hoop your students jump through.

The student must sit quietly in time-out while doing the work you’ve assigned—even if it’s simply paying attention to your lesson. If he (or she) does what you ask during those first fifteen minutes, then stroll by and whisper, “Let me know when you’re ready to return to your seat.
The onus is on the student, not you. This is where the power of time-out comes from–that is, with the burden of responsibility resting solely on his shoulders.
Time-out means nothing and does nothing unless your students are affected by the experience. They have to care.
